title: AN ACT to amend the act Appropriating Money, passed at this session of the General Assembly.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 1327, p. 116
summary: This act amends a previous appropriation act to increase the daily pay for the services of a 'negro boy' to wait upon the Senate from $1.25 to $1.50.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 648, pp. 293–296
title: AN ACT authorizing the County Court of Gallatin county to Levya Tax to raise a Recruiting Fund to avoid a Draft in said county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 648, pp. 293–296
summary: This act authorizes county courts to levy taxes and issue bonds to fund a recruiting fund. It specifically allows for a poll tax on "white male citizens and free male colored persons over the age of twenty-one years" or on "white and colored males within the military ages, to-wit: between the age of twenty and forty-five years, and not now in the service."

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 695, pp. 42–43
title: AN ACT to regulate the Fees of Justices of the Peace.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 695, pp. 42–43
summary: This act outlines the fees for various services provided by Justices of the Peace in Kentucky. Notably, it includes specific fees for actions related to slaves, such as arresting and carrying a slave before a justice, and whipping a slave by order of an officer. These provisions, while framed as fee regulations, directly address the legal and penal treatment of enslaved individuals, reflecting the racial hierarchy and control mechanisms prevalent during the post-Civil War era, which continued into the Jim Crow period.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 796, pp. 400–401
title: AN ACT for the benefit of Thos.M. Hicks.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 796, pp. 400–401
summary: This act directs the Auditor of Public Accounts to issue a warrant to Thomas M. Hicks for $671.70, payable from the runaway slave fund. This is compensation for a negro woman and her child who were purchased by Hicks but later taken by U.S. military authorities. Hicks must provide bond to indemnify the state and pay the former owner if they prove ownership and claim proceeds from runaway slaves.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 942, pp. 507–510
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled"An act to incorporate the town of Mt. Sterling," approved March 12, 1851, and an act to amend an act, entitled "An act to incorporate Mount Sterling," approved February28,1863.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, ch. 942, pp. 507–510
summary: This section of the statute outlines the qualifications for voters in the town of Mount Sterling. It explicitly states that voters must be 'white male citizens' over the age of twenty-one, with specific residency requirements. It also includes an additional category of voters: 'white male citizens' who live outside the town but within Montgomery county, provided they own real estate within Mount Sterling subject to taxation.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, p. 197
title: RESOLUTION requesting the President to withdraw Negro Troops from the State of Kentucky
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1865, p. 197
summary: This resolution requests the Governor to urge the President to immediately remove all "negro troops" from Kentucky. The justification provided is that their presence is detrimental to citizens, they commit outrages, and their presence causes irritation to former owners and citizens. The resolution also requests that white soldiers be assigned for duty in their place.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1865, ch. 1227, p. 166
title: AN ACT to prevent the destruction of fish in Rockcastle river and tributaries.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1865, ch. 1227, p. 166
summary: This act prohibits seining or netting for fish in Rockcastle river and its tributaries, making it a misdemeanor punishable by a fine. Crucially, it specifies that if a slave is convicted of violating this act, they shall be punished by whipping, not exceeding thirty-nine stripes. This differential punishment based on enslaved status is a clear indicator of racial discrimination.

citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, p. 145
summary: This act establishes the fees that constables can charge for various services. Notably, it includes specific fees for 'arresting and carrying a slave before a justice of the peace or other officer' and 'whipping a slave by order of an officer of competent authority'.

statute_citation: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, p. 18
title: AN ACT to amend the act approved third March, 1863, entitled "An act to amend fifth article of chapter eighty-six, of the Revised Statutes."* 11 SEC. I. That the act approved third March, 1863, entitled, "an act to amend fifth article of chapter eighty-six, of the Revised Statutes," be so amended as…
citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, p. 18
summary: This act amends the Master and Apprentice law. It repeals Section 5 of Article 1, Chapter 64 of the Revised Statutes. The new law specifies that apprenticeship writings must be signed by the master and for the minor by the county court clerk. It details the requirements for teaching, feeding, clothing, and humane treatment of apprentices. Crucially, it differentiates the obligations based on the apprentice's race: if the apprentice is not a negro, the master must teach them to read and write and common arithmetic. If the apprentice is a negro, the master is bound to pay the apprentice a sum of money ($50 for a girl, $100 for a boy) at the end of the apprenticeship, unless the master teaches them to read and write, in which case the payment is waived.

summary: This act confers civil rights upon negroes and mulattoes, allowing them to sue and be sued, acquire and dispose of property, and make affidavits in judicial proceedings as white persons may. It also explicitly prohibits intermarriage between negroes/mulattoes and white persons, deeming it a felony punishable by imprisonment in the state penitentiary for at least five years. The act defines who is considered a negro or mulatto.

title: AN ACT to amend the common school law, defining the number of days in a school month.
citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 26–28
summary: This act amends existing statutes concerning negroes and mulattoes. It repeals several sections related to the Revised Statutes concerning these groups, including those dealing with runaway slaves and fees for their arrest. It also amends other sections to make all negroes and mulattoes liable to the same punishments and triable in the same manner as free negroes, with specific sections repealed or amended to apply to all negroes and mulattoes.

statute_citation: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, p. 28
title: AN ACT to revise, amend, and reduce into one the common school laws of Kentucky. ##
citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, p. 28
summary: This act consolidates and revises the common school laws of Kentucky. It establishes the 'school fund' and outlines the auditor's duties in managing its accounts and making annual apportionments. Crucially, Section III of Article I specifies that the apportionment of the school fund among counties and districts is based on the number of 'free white children' between the ages of six and twenty. Later sections (specifically SEC. VI) detail the distribution of a separate fund for 'common schools for negroes and mulattoes,' indicating a racially segregated system.

citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 50–52

The bond and oath are to be taken before the county court, which must approve the sureties and be satisfied of the coffee-house keeper's good character.

citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 68–72
summary: This act mandates that tax assessors in Kentucky must ascertain and return the number of free persons of color in their respective counties, reporting this information in a separate column on their lists. The act was to take effect on January 1, 1861.

statute_citation: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 72–74
title: AN ACT authorizing the commissioners of the sinking fund to contract with the state banks for interest on state deposits.
citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 72–74
summary: This act mandates that no slave can be emancipated unless a bond is posted to ensure the slave is removed from the state within ninety days. The emancipated slave must also sign a statement abandoning their residence in the state. Failure to comply with this covenant will result in legal action for damages, with a minimum damage amount set at the slave's value at the time of emancipation. Attorneys prosecuting such cases receive 20% of the damages, and informers receive $10.

statute_citation: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 74–76
title: AN ACT authorizing the board of managers of the Western Lunatic Asylum to appoint a superintendent of said institution. SEC. I. That the board of managers of the Western Lunatic Asylum, be and they are hereby authorized, when the same in their opinion is necessary, to appoint a superintendent for…
citations: A Digest of the General Laws of Kentucky, 1866, pp. 74–76
summary: This act amends existing statutes regarding the appointment of managers for lunatic asylums and the appointment and duties of superintendents for the Western Lunatic Asylum. It specifies how vacancies in the board of managers are filled and outlines the qualifications, salary, and removal powers for the superintendent. The text also includes sections on divorce proceedings and militia organization, but the most relevant part for Jim Crow analysis is the section concerning free negroes and mulattoes being deemed guilty of felony if they come into the state with the intention of remaining, or come for any purpose other than obedience to court process, with penalties including penitentiary confinement and potential life imprisonment for re-entry after release on bond.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 556, p. 78
title: AN ACT in relation to the marriage of negroes and mulattoes.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 556, p. 78
summary: This act regulates the marriage of Black individuals in Kentucky. It allows Black individuals to marry each other under the same regulations as white persons, with separate record-keeping. It also validates existing cohabiting relationships and their issue. Crucially, it prohibits interracial marriage between Black and white individuals, making it a felony punishable by at least five years in the state penitentiary. The act defines 'negroes and mulattoes' based on ancestry.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 603, pp. 84–85
title: AN ACT repealing and amending certain sections, articles, and chapters of the Revised Statutes and Session Acts approved since the adoption of the Re vised Statutes, concerning slaves and free negroes.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 603, pp. 84–85
summary: This act repeals or amends various sections of the Revised Statutes and Session Acts related to slaves and free negroes. Specifically, it repeals articles on patrols, the listing of slaves, and provisions for whipping slaves. It also amends a section to remove the penalty of whipping for a free person and a slave, and repeals sections related to runaway slaves and makes all negroes and mulattoes liable to certain provisions.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 621, pp. 90–91
title: AN ACT to amend article1, chapter64, Revised Statutes, title"Master and Apprentice."
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 621, pp. 90–91
summary: This act amends the Master and Apprentice law. It repeals Section 5 of Article 1, Chapter 64 of the Revised Statutes. The new Section 2 outlines the requirements for apprenticeship contracts, including the age of the minor, the trade to be taught, medical attention, food, clothing, and humane treatment. Crucially, it specifies that if the apprentice is not a negro, the master must teach them to read, write, and common arithmetic. If the apprentice *is* a negro, the master is bound to pay them at the end of the apprenticeship, implying a different standard of education or compensation based on race.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 636, p. 92
title: AN ACT for the benefit of the negroes and mulattoes in this Commonwealth.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 636, p. 92
summary: This act establishes a separate fund from taxes collected from negroes and mulattoes for their benefit. Half of this fund is designated for the support of their paupers, and the remainder for the education of their children. It mandates a $2 poll tax on male negroes and mulattoes over 18, requires separate record-keeping for their taxable property, and allows for separate schools for negro and mulatto children. Paupers are to be supported from this fund based on county court certifications.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 672, p. 93
title: AN ACT in relation to contracts with negroes and mulattoes.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 672, p. 93
summary: This act allows parties in labor contracts between white persons and negroes or mulattoes to stipulate that the contract is entire. If either party abandons the contract without good cause, the other party is considered to have completed their part. All such contracts must be in writing and attested by a white person.

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 770, p. 825
summary: This act revives and re-enacts a previous act incorporating the town of Stamping Ground. It modifies the election of trustees and specifies that the capitation tax authorized in a previous section shall be assessed, levied, and collected from all white citizens and resident negroes or mulattoes twenty-one years of age.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 818, pp. 107–108
title: AN ACT to amend the vagrant laws.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 818, pp. 107–108
summary: This act defines vagrancy as being an able-bodied person loitering without means of support, not laboring, or abandoning a family without provision. Convicted vagrants are to be apprehended, tried, and if found guilty, sentenced to labor for a period not exceeding twelve months. Those over twenty-one are to be sent to houses of correction, or if none exist, a superintendent will be appointed by the county court to oversee their labor.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 881, pp. 109–110
title: AN ACT to regulate coffee-houses in this Commonwealth.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, ch. 881, pp. 109–110
summary: This act requires coffee-house keepers to execute a bond and take an oath before selling spirituous or vinous liquors. The bond is conditioned on keeping an orderly house, not selling to disorderly or intoxicated persons, and specifically not selling to any minor or freenegro in violation of the laws of the Commonwealth. The county court must approve the bond and be satisfied of the keeper's good character.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, p. 129
title: RESOLUTIONS concerning the Freedmen's Bureau and charges against General Fisk
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1866, p. 129
summary: These resolutions from the Kentucky General Assembly in 1866 request the withdrawal of military forces and the Freedmen's Bureau from the state. They state the legislature's intent to enact laws for the 'colored population' that are just and humane, suited to their 'present condition,' and provide necessary protection. The resolutions also authorize a committee to investigate charges against General C. B. Fisk and report their findings to the Governor and President. A separate resolution rescinds the tenth joint rule of the two Houses.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1433, pp. 616–639
title: AN ACT to reduce into one, amend, and digest the acts and amend a tory acts incorporating the City of Lexington. City Incorporated.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1433, pp. 616–639

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1562, pp. 83–84

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1562, pp. 83–84

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1661, pp. 91–92

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1661, pp. 91–92
summary: This act amends Chapter 34 of the Revised Statutes concerning Escheats and Escheators. It specifies that if a free person of color dies intestate, and their heirs would have inherited but were previously held in slavery, or if a free person of color dies leaving a will that bequeaths property to individuals who were previously held in slavery, these heirs, legatees, and devisees (or their heirs) are now competent to inherit or receive the property.

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1882, p. 122
summary: This act directs the Auditor of Public Accounts to issue warrants for the care of 'lunatics of color' sent to the Lunatic Asylum, provided certain conditions are met, similar to the process for white persons. statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1913, pp. 125–127
title: AN ACT for the benefit of the Negroes and Mulattoes of this Commonwealth.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 1913, pp. 125–127
summary: This act levies an additional tax of two dollars on every male negro and mulatto over eighteen years of age. The collected funds are to be used exclusively for the support of negro and mulatto paupers and the education of negro and mulatto children within the county where the tax was collected. It mandates separate tax columns for negroes and mulattoes and outlines the process for allocating funds to negro schools, including per-scholar allowances and reporting requirements.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 2002, p. 131

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, ch. 2002, p. 131

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 575
title: AN ACT to amend the 10th article of the Charter of the City of Louisville.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 575
summary: This act amends the charter of the City of Louisville's public school system. It allows non-resident taxpayers to send their children to city schools free of tuition, but explicitly prohibits children of the African race from attending schools with white children. statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1867, ch. 1762, p. 346

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1867, ch. 1762, p. 346

Crucially, it explicitly states that the colored population of the district shall not be included in the tax and that colored children shall not be admitted to the common school of the district. The act requires a vote of qualified voters for its adoption.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1867, ch. 1887, pp. 450–456

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1867, ch. 1887, pp. 450–456
summary: This section of the act grants the general council of Louisville the power to establish and maintain a 'house of reform for white females'. statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1867, ch. 2091, pp. 617–618
title: AN ACT for the benefit of William O. Murrell, of Adair County.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2 [Local and Private Acts], 1867, ch. 2091, pp. 617–618

This specific example demonstrates the legal framework for property disputes involving enslaved or formerly enslaved individuals, reflecting the post-slavery but still racially stratified legal landscape of the era.

statute_citation: The Code of Practice in Civil and Criminal Cases for the State of Kentucky, 1867, § 656, pp. 211–215
title: SEC. 656. *Order in which proof to be given on trial.* The party who begins the case must ordinarily exhaust his evidence before the other begins.
citations: The Code of Practice in Civil and Criminal Cases for the State of Kentucky, 1867, § 656, pp. 211–215
summary: This statute outlines who is competent to testify in civil actions. It lists several categories of individuals who are incompetent, including those convicted of certain crimes, infants under ten, those of unsound mind, spouses, attorneys, persons with an interest in the issue, and 'Negroes, etc.'. All other objections to a witness's testimony are to be considered as affecting their credibility.

statute_citation: The Code of Practice in Civil and Criminal Cases for the State of Kentucky, 1867, § 9, pp. 589–591
title: SEC.9. Modes of preventing offenses.
citations: The Code of Practice in Civil and Criminal Cases for the State of Kentucky, 1867, § 9, pp. 589–591
summary: This statute outlines the criminal jurisdiction of justices' courts and city/police courts in Kentucky. It specifies the types of misdemeanors and offenses these courts can hear, differentiating penalties based on whether the accused is a 'free person' or a 'slave'. It also details concurrent and exclusive jurisdiction with circuit courts and allows for the removal of cases from circuit court to lower courts. An amendment from 1856 is also included, which repeals exclusive jurisdiction of justices of the peace over surveyors of public roads and grants circuit courts jurisdiction over such cases.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 187
title: The New Constitution of Kentucky
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 187
summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines provisions related to slavery, including the emancipation of slaves, restrictions on their presence in the state after emancipation, and the prevention of slave importation. It also grants power to the legislature to ensure the humane treatment of slaves by their owners.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 242
title: Liability for Conveying Slaves Out of State
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 242
summary: This statute establishes liability for steamboats and other vessels that transport slaves out of the state or from one part of the state to another without the owner's written consent, or without the owner or rightful controller of the slave being a passenger. It also makes the captain and owner personally liable. The statute explicitly mentions 'slaves,' indicating its context within the antebellum and immediate post-bellum period concerning enslaved people.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 243
title: An Act to Prevent the Removal of Slaves Out of This State
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 243
summary: This statute makes it illegal to transport a slave out of the state of Kentucky or from one point within the state to another on a boat. Violators face fines and/or imprisonment. The statute also outlines procedures for enforcing liens and liabilities related to such actions, including the use of attachments and bonds. Case law clarifies that the statute applies to slaves subject to Kentucky laws and not those escaping from other states.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 293
title: CONSTABLES.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 293
summary: This statute outlines the duties and responsibilities of constables in Kentucky, including their oath of office, the process for vacating their office, and the types of legal processes they are authorized to execute. Notably, it includes a provision stating that constables 'Shall whip slaves under the orders of justices of the peace.'

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 414
title: CRIMES AND PUNISHMENTS
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 414
summary: This section of the Revised Statutes of Kentucky (1867) outlines fees for commonwealth's attorneys based on fines assessed for various offenses, including gaming, operating a tippling house, and standing horses without a license. It also specifies how fines and forfeitures can be recovered. Crucially, Section XXVI states that the provisions of this chapter shall not apply to slaves, except where specifically named, nor to free negroes when punishment for the same offense is provided elsewhere in the Revised Statutes. This creates a differential application of criminal law based on race.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 415
title: Conspiracy of white person with negro.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 415
summary: This statute criminalizes a free white person who advises, counsels, or conspires with a negro (bond or free) to rebel or make insurrection against their master or the laws. The punishment is death or confinement in the penitentiary for six to ten years.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 419
title: Carnally knowing white girl under ten years, or an idiot. Abducting unmarried white girl under fourteen years. Taking or detaining white woman against her will, with intent to marry or carnally know.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 419
summary: This statute outlines criminal offenses related to sexual assault and abduction, specifically mentioning 'white girls' and 'white women'. It prescribes penalties for carnally knowing a white girl under ten or an idiot, abducting an unmarried white girl under fourteen, and taking or detaining a white woman against her will with intent to marry or have carnal knowledge. The explicit mention of 'white' in relation to victims suggests a racial distinction in the application of these laws, which is characteristic of Jim Crow era legislation that often codified racial hierarchies.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 441
title: Selling, purchasing, or removing from state negro entitled to freedom in future, without consent of court.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 441
summary: This statute prohibits the sale, purchase, or removal from Kentucky of any negro who is entitled to future freedom, without the consent of the county or circuit court. It specifies penalties including fines and imprisonment, and outlines the requirements for court authorization.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 450
title: Crimes and Punishments - Differential Penalties for Free Negroes and Slaves
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 450
summary: This section of the Revised Statutes of Kentucky (1867) outlines penalties for various offenses. Notably, it specifies differential punishments for 'free negroes' and 'slaves' compared to other persons for certain crimes, including the use of sickening or intoxicating substances and the killing, disfiguring, or maiming of animals. Free negroes and slaves could receive corporal punishment (stripes) where others would receive fines or imprisonment.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 454
title: An Act to amend the law in relation to Crimes and Punishments.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 454
summary: This act amends the Revised Statutes concerning arson and burning of buildings. It specifically addresses the willful and unlawful burning of vehicles by any person, whether white, free negro, slave, or other. It states that such an offender shall be punished in the same manner as prescribed for other arson offenses, with a specific provision that a slave offender shall be punished by any number of stripes not exceeding one hundred.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 581
title: Liability of owners, etc., for transporting slaves.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 581
summary: This statute imposes a significant financial penalty on ferry owners and keepers if they transport a slave across the Ohio River without the slave owner's explicit consent or accompaniment. The penalty is $200, and if the transport is done with the knowledge or assent of the ferry owner/keeper, the penalty increases to $1000, recoverable by any prosecutor. This indicates a legal framework that treated enslaved people as property and regulated their movement, reflecting the racial hierarchy of the time.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 597
title: FUGITIVES FROM JUSTICE. ARTICLE II. ARREST OF PERSONS FOR OFFENSES COMMITTED IN ANOTHER STATE OR TERRITORY.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 597
summary: This statute outlines the process for arresting and detaining individuals accused of felonies committed in other states or territories, and for dealing with persons accused of abducting people of color from Kentucky. Specifically, it requires judges to inquire into the ownership or agency of the accused in cases involving the abduction of a person of color, and to discharge the accused if they acted with the owner's sanction. Otherwise, they are to be dealt with according to the chapter's provisions. For felonies committed elsewhere, individuals found in Kentucky can be arrested and confined, then delivered to the proper authorities upon demand from the executive of the state or territory where the offense occurred.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 607
title: GAMING. - SEC. XXV. Fine for a white person gaming with a free negro or slave.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 607
summary: This section of the statutes imposes a fine of not more than fifty dollars on any white person who plays cards, dice, or any other game for money or other valuable thing with a free negro or slave. The fine is to be paid by the white person.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 611
title: An Act to amend the forty-second chapter of the Revised Statutes.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 611
summary: This act imposes penalties on free Black individuals for gaming with slaves or white persons, and on white persons for gaming with Black individuals or mulattoes. It also disqualifies white persons convicted of playing cards with Black individuals or mulattoes from holding office and serving on juries. Penalties include fines and imprisonment.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 612
title: GAMING. SEC. III. - SEC. V.
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, p. 612
summary: This statute criminalizes any free negro playing games with any white person, free negro, or slave. It also establishes a presumption of being a free man for those accused under this section, requiring rebuttal. An amendment clarifies that billiard tables for private family amusement are exempt.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 10, pp. 99–102
title: SEC. 10. And be it further enacted, That when any person held to service or labor in any state or territory, or in the district of Columbia, shall escape therefrom, the party to whom such service or labor shall be due, his, her, or their agent or attorney may apply to any court of record therein, or…
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 10, pp. 99–102
summary: This statute outlines the process for apprehending and returning fugitives from labor (enslaved people) to their state of origin. It details the evidence required for arrest, the authority of officers to use force to prevent rescue, and the compensation for officers and their assistants. The statute also specifies that a transcript of a court record, authenticated by the clerk and seal, serves as conclusive evidence of escape and the debt of service or labor in any other state.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 1, p. 140

citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 1, p. 140; The General Statutes of Kentucky, 1879, § 1, pp. 108–109; The General Statutes of Kentucky, 1887, § 1, pp. 107–108; The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1, p. 78

It prohibits laws for emancipation without owner consent or compensation, allows emigrants to bring slaves, permits owners to emancipate slaves under certain conditions, and grants the assembly power to restrict slave importation. It also mandates laws for the humane treatment of slaves and allows for their sale if owners neglect this. Crucially, it states that grand juries are not necessary for prosecuting slaves for felony, though they retain the right to an impartial trial by a petit jury.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 1, pp. 188–189
title: SEC. 1. The capital of the fund called and known as the "common school fund," consisting of one million two hundred and twenty-five thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight dollars and forty-two cents, for which bonds have been executed by the state to the board of education, and seventy-three…

Section 3 outlines that grand juries are not necessary for prosecuting slaves for felonies, but they retain the right to an impartial trial by a petit jury.

The election shall be held at the same time…

It also allows immigrants to bring their slaves into the state.

It also mandates laws for the humane treatment of slaves and allows for their sale if owners neglect this. Crucially, it states that grand juries are not necessary for prosecuting slaves for felony, though they retain the right to an impartial trial by a petit jury.

Section 3 outlines that grand juries are not necessary for prosecuting slaves for felonies, but they retain the right to an impartial trial by a petit jury.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 3, p. 93
title: SEC. 3. *And be it also enacted*, That when a person held to labor in any of the United States, or in either of the territories on the north-west or south of the river Ohio, under the laws thereof, shall escape into any other of the said states or territories, the person to whom such labor or…
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 3, p. 93
summary: This statute outlines the process for apprehending and returning fugitives from labor (enslaved people) to their rightful owners. It empowers agents to transport fugitives and imposes penalties on those who rescue or harbor them. The process involves presenting proof of ownership to a judge or magistrate, who then issues a certificate for removal.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 5, pp. 95–96
title: SEC. 5. *And be it further enacted*, That it shall be the duty of all marshals and deputy marshals to obey and execute all warrants and precepts issued under the provisions of this act, when to them directed; and should any marshal or deputy marshal refuse to receive such warrant, or other process…
citations: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 5, pp. 95–96
summary: This statute outlines the process for reclaiming fugitives from labor. It grants commissioners concurrent jurisdiction with federal judges to issue certificates for the removal of such fugitives. It also mandates marshals and deputy marshals to execute warrants related to these fugitives, with penalties for refusal or escape. Commissioners are authorized to appoint individuals to execute these warrants and to summon bystanders or the posse comitatus for assistance.

statute_citation: The Revised Statutes of Kentucky, v. 1, 1867, § 6, pp. 96–97
title: SEC. 6.
