citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 965, pp. 1174–1176
summary: This statute outlines the land description for the Colored Normal School, indicating a separate educational institution for Black individuals, which reflects the segregationist policies of the Jim Crow era.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 967, pp. 1178–1206
title: AN ACT to regulate municipal elections in city of Bowling Green.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 967, pp. 1178–1206
summary: This statute outlines the responsibilities of the mayor regarding the preparation and security of election materials, including ballots and stubs, with strict measures to prevent unauthorized access to these materials. It emphasizes the control of election processes, which historically has been used to disenfranchise Black voters.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 968, pp. 1206–1214
title: AN ACT to provide for the registration of voters in the city of Bowling Green.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 968, pp. 1206–1214
summary: This statute outlines the appointment and duties of registration officers in Bowling Green, emphasizing that only voters and housekeepers in the precinct can serve. It includes provisions for maintaining order and verifying the qualifications of individuals seeking to register, which could be used to disenfranchise certain groups.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 974, pp. 1216–1221
title: AN ACT authorizing the establishment of a graded free school in district number sixteen, Fulton county, Kentucky.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 974, pp. 1216–1221
summary: This statute establishes a tax levy specifically for white voters in a designated school district to fund a graded free school and pay off bonds for Hickman College, effectively excluding non-white individuals from participating in the tax and educational benefits.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 978, pp. 1228–1234
title: AN ACT to establish a system of public graded schools in the city of Pineville.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 978, pp. 1228–1234
summary: This statute establishes a public graded school system in Pineville, Kentucky, specifically for white children, controlled by trustees elected by qualified white voters, thereby enforcing racial segregation in education.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 984, pp. 1253–1282
title: AN ACT to regulate municipal elections in the city of Paducah.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 984, pp. 1253–1282
summary: This statute outlines the procedures for municipal elections, including the nomination of candidates, the printing of ballots, and the responsibilities of the mayor and election officers. It emphasizes the need for strict control over election materials to prevent tampering.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 996, pp. 1307–1313
title: AN ACT to establish a public graded school at the mouth of Beaver, in Floyd county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 996, pp. 1307–1313
summary: This statute establishes the Mouth of Beaver Graded Free School and outlines its governance by a board of trustees elected exclusively by white qualified voters, indicating a racially discriminatory practice in educational governance.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 997, pp. 1314–1316
title: AN ACT for the benefit of the University Club of Louisville.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 2, 1890, ch. 997, pp. 1314–1316
summary: This statute incorporates the University Club of Louisville, establishing it as a body corporate with specific membership and stock ownership rules that implicitly restrict membership to certain demographics.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1222, p. 53
title: AN ACT to allow the citizens of this Commonwealth to meet, organize, hold lodge meetings or religious services in the district school-houses of this State.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1222, p. 53
summary: This act grants citizens the right to use district schoolhouses for meetings and religious services, provided it does not conflict with school operations. Crucially, it explicitly states that white citizens cannot use schoolhouses intended for colored children, and vice versa. This provision is limited to Marshall and Lyon counties.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1268, pp. 174–175
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled" An act to incorporate an institution of learning in or near Cadiz, in the county of Trigg," approved April sixteenth, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1268, pp. 174–175
summary: This act amends a previous act concerning the town of Trigg. It replaces the name 'Cadiz Graded Colored School' with 'The Baptist Normal Institute' and updates the corresponding 'Trustees of the Cadiz Graded School' to 'Trustees of the Baptist Normal Institute'.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1340, pp. 379–387
title: AN ACT to provide for a registration of voters in the city of Owensboro.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1340, pp. 379–387
summary: This statute mandates the creation of two registration books for each precinct in Owensboro. One book is kept in the registrar's office, and the other is provided to registration and election clerks. The books are to be arranged alphabetically by voter name and include columns for 'NAME', 'Residence', 'Special Elections', 'December Election', 'August Election', 'Color', and 'Remarks'. Section 5 details the registration process, requiring officers to attend voting places on the first Monday in July and the two succeeding days, from 6 AM to 7 PM. They are to record qualified voters who apply, noting their name, residence (including street and number), and whether they are 'white or colored'. The statute also includes a provision to omit a registration day if it falls on the fourth of the month.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1427, pp. 522–524
title: AN ACT to establish a graded school in common school district number one, in Leslie county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1427, pp. 522–524
summary: This act establishes a graded school in district number one of Leslie County, Kentucky. It outlines the boundaries of the district, the style and powers of the board of trustees, and specifies that the board shall be elected by white voters of the district. It also states that all white pupils between the ages of six and twenty residing in the district are eligible to attend.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1431, p. 534
title: AN ACT to authorize district number eighty-three, in Barren county, to vote a tax for three years for the purpose of extending the session of said school.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1431, p. 534
summary: This act authorizes the trustees of white common school district number eighty-three in Barren county to submit a proposition to legal white voters. The proposition is to assess a tax for three years of twenty-five cents on each one hundred dollars of white taxable property and a per capita tax of one dollar on each white legal voter annually. The purpose of this tax is to extend the school session by at least three months each year.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1460, pp. 583–588
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled"An act to establish a system of common schools for the town of Beech Grove; McLean county," approved April twenty-two, one thousand eight hundred and eighty—two, and to repeal an act amend a tory there to, approved March twenty—five, one thousand eight hundred and…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1460, pp. 583–588
summary: This act amends the establishment of a board of education for the Louisville district. It outlines the election process for board members, their powers and duties, and the appointment of an assessor. Crucially, Section 4 explicitly states that the assessor's duty is to 'take a list of all property of white persons in said district subject to taxation for the State revenue.'

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1487, pp. 696–697
title: AN ACT for the benefit of E. L. Garnett, James Carman and John W. Wrather, late trustees in and for common school district number forty-two, Graves county, Kentucky. -
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1487, pp. 696–697
summary: This act empowers the trustees of district number forty-two to levy a poll-tax on legal white voters and a property tax to pay for desks and seats purchased for the district, and to reimburse individuals for costs incurred in a legal dispute over the election and the purchase. It also orders the sheriff to refund collected tax money.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1517, pp. 791–793
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled"An act to incorporate the Williamsburg Institute," approved April sixth, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1517, pp. 791–793
summary: This statute incorporates an institute and grants it powers related to property, contracts, and operations. Crucially, it explicitly states that 'none but white pupils shall ever be admitted in the school of said institute.'

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1528, pp. 804–805
title: AN ACT for the benefit of common school districts numbers thirty—three and thirty-four, of Henderson county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1528, pp. 804–805
summary: This act authorizes the trustees of consolidated common school districts numbers thirty-three and thirty-four in Henderson County, Kentucky, to submit to the qualified white voters of said districts a proposition regarding the districts. The submission is to occur at a general or special election, with thirty days' notice given by publication in local newspapers or by posting written or printed notices.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1572, pp. 957–1000
title: AN ACT to incorporate the city of Maysville, in Mason county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1572, pp. 957–1000
summary: This section of the statute outlines the duties of the city assessor in Louisville, Kentucky, for the year 1890. It mandates that the assessor maintain two separate lists or books for property assessment: one for white individuals and one for black individuals. The statute details the information to be included in these assessment lists, such as names, age, property descriptions, and values of various assets.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1606, pp. 1104–1116
title: AN ACT to provide for a registration of voters in the city of Co ving- 1 ton.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1606, pp. 1104–1116
summary: This statute outlines the process for general voter registration in Kentucky for the year 1890. It specifies the dates and hours for registration, the information to be recorded in the registration book (including name, address, and whether the person is white or colored), and the qualifications for registration. It also details a provision for omitting a registration day if it falls on the fourth of the month.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1657, pp. 1223–1225
title: AN ACT for the benefit of white school district number twenty-eight, of Madison county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1657, pp. 1223–1225
summary: This act authorizes the trustees of a specific white school district in Madison County to issue bonds up to $20,000 for building and furnishing schoolhouses. It also establishes a tax mechanism to redeem these bonds and pay interest. The statute explicitly mentions 'white' school district and begins to discuss the assessment of property for 'colored people' in the last sentence, indicating a racial distinction in the application of the law or its context.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1658, p. 1225
title: AN ACT for the benefit of Bedford common school district number six(white), in Trimble county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1658, p. 1225
summary: This act empowers the trustees of Bedford common school district number six (white) in Trimble county to levy an additional annual property tax and poll tax for two years, not exceeding twenty-five cents per one hundred dollars of taxable property and one dollar per white poll, respectively. These funds are specifically for repairing and furnishing the common school-house of said district.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1760, pp. 1412–1427
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled"An act to reduce into one, amend and digest the acts and amend a tory acts incorporating the city of Mount Sterling," approved March seventh, one thousand eighth un—dred and seventy-six.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1760, pp. 1412–1427
summary: This statute outlines the process for voter registration in Mount Sterling, Kentucky. It mandates the use of registration books with specific columns, including 'Color'. Registration officers are required to attend voting places for two days to register qualified voters who personally appear. The statute also details procedures for swearing in and interrogating potential registrants if their identity or qualifications are questioned.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1785, pp. 1497–1500
title: AN ACT to incorporate the "C. T. Rice Cemetery Company," near Union, in Boone county.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1785, pp. 1497–1500
summary: This act incorporates the Evergreen Cemetery Company and outlines its powers and regulations. Notably, Section 13 explicitly prohibits the interment of colored persons in any lot within the cemetery, with forfeiture of the lot and improvements for any owner who attempts such an interment. The company is also empowered to prohibit such interments.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1809, pp. 1543–1547
title: AN ACT to incorporate the Ekron Male and Female College, of Meade county, Kentucky.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, v. 3 [Local and Private Acts], 1890, ch. 1809, pp. 1543–1547
summary: This act details the funding and operation of a common school in the Ekron common school district. It specifies that a tax levy can be imposed, collected by the sheriff, and used exclusively for maintaining the common school. Crucially, it states that 'every white child in the Ekron common school district between the ages of six and twenty years shall have the right to attend the said common school'.

statute_citation: Kentucky Jurisprudence, 1890, p. 228
title: Devolution of Landed Estates
citations: Kentucky Jurisprudence, 1890, p. 228
summary: This section of the Kentucky statutes, from 1890, discusses inheritance laws. Specifically, point 6 states that the issue of a marriage between a white person and a negro or mulatto is void. This explicitly addresses and prohibits interracial marriage.

statute_citation: Kentucky Jurisprudence, 1890, p. 542
title: Marriage and Divorce
citations: Kentucky Jurisprudence, 1890, p. 542
summary: This statute outlines the requirements and conditions for marriage and divorce in Kentucky. It addresses the legalization of cohabitation for former slaves, the authority of ministers to solemnize marriages, void marriages due to incestuous relationships, idiocy, lunacy, or bigamy. Crucially, it explicitly states that a marriage is void 'between a white person and a negro or mulatto (less than one eighth of negro blood not being considered)'.

statute_citation: Kentucky Jurisprudence, 1890, p. 713
title: Tax on Negroes for Common Schools
citations: Kentucky Jurisprudence, 1890, p. 713
summary: This statute discusses a case where a tax was levied on 'negroes' to fund common schools. The court held this law unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment, implying that the collection of this tax was unauthorized. The case highlights the discriminatory nature of funding public education based on race, which is a hallmark of Jim Crow era legislation.

statute_citation: Constitution of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, § 185, pp. 53–54
title: SEC. 185. The General Assembly shall make provision, by law, for the payment of the interest of said school fund, and may provide for the sale of the stock in the Bank of Kentucky; and in case of a sale of all or any part of said stock, the proceeds of sale shall be invested by the Sinking Fund…
citations: Constitution of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, § 185, pp. 53–54
summary: This section mandates that in the distribution of the school fund, no distinction shall be made on account of race or color, but explicitly states that separate schools for white and colored children shall be maintained.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 103, pp. 304–393
title: AN ACT relating to Revenue and Taxation.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 103, pp. 304–393
summary: This statute amends an existing act concerning railroad taxation. Specifically, it addresses how taxes levied in common school districts are to be distributed. Section 6 explicitly states that the provisions of the law shall not apply to any colored school district, but then outlines a method for distributing railroad taxes between white and colored common school districts located within the same boundaries. This distribution is to be based on the ratio of white to colored children of pupil age residing in the district.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 117, pp. 420–423
title: AN ACT to establish a board of children'sguardians in counties in which thereis a city of the first class, defining the powers and duties of said board, and providing for a special county tax for the establishment and maintenance of homes under the care of such board.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 117, pp. 420–423
summary: This act establishes a board of children's guardians in counties with a first-class city. The board is to be composed of six persons, two of whom shall be colored. The board will be a corporate body responsible for children's welfare and will be funded by a special county tax.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 205, pp. 952–968
title: AN ACT relating to husband and wife, and entitled"Husband and Wife."
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 205, pp. 952–968
summary: This act outlines prohibited marriages, including those between a white person and a negro or mulatto. It also details other grounds for void marriages, such as mental incapacity, existing marriages, and improper solemnization.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 211, pp. 990–993
title: AN ACT concerning the State Normal School for Colored Persons.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 211, pp. 990–993
summary: This act places the State Normal School for Colored Persons under the control and supervision of a board of trustees. The board will consist of the Superintendent of Public Instruction as ex officio chairman and three appointed residents of Franklin county. The board is constituted as a body corporate with the power to sue and be sued, and to hold funds and property for the school.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 222, pp. 1092–1154
title: AN ACT for the government of cities of the third class.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 222, pp. 1092–1154
summary: This statute mandates that the board of education provide separate buildings and schools for the education of white and black pupils, explicitly prohibiting white children from attending colored schools and colored children from attending white schools.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 239, pp. 1236–1237
title: AN ACT to empower the trustees of the State Normal School for Colored Persons at Frankfort to build a dormitory.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 239, pp. 1236–1237
summary: This act authorizes the trustees of the State Normal School for Colored Persons at Frankfort to build a dormitory for students attending the school. It also appropriates $2,000 for its construction.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 241, pp. 1238–1283
title: AN ACT for the government of cities of the fourth class.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 241, pp. 1238–1283
summary: This statute mandates that cities provide separate buildings and schools for the education of white and black pupils, explicitly prohibiting white children from attending colored schools and vice versa. It also outlines administrative duties for the board of education.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 244, pp. 1292–1370
title: AN ACT for the government of cities of the first class.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 244, pp. 1292–1370
summary: This section mandates the segregation of schools by race, stating that no white child shall attend a school for colored children, and no colored child shall attend a school for white children. Schools for both races must be kept and maintained separately.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 246, pp. 1371–1372
title: AN ACT to provide for the levy and collection of a tax in certain common school districts to pay off indebtedness incurred by the trustees of such school districts in erecting and furnishing school -houses.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 246, pp. 1371–1372
summary: This act amends a previous act concerning the State Penitentiary. It allows the Commissioners of the Sinking Fund to purchase materials and employ prisoners for construction and repairs at the penitentiary. It also declares an emergency due to idle prisoners, making the act effective immediately upon passage. However, a separate section from the same source document, likely a preceding or following section on the same page, states that no tax shall be levied or collected from the property of colored persons to pay any indebtedness incurred for the benefit of schools for white children.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 260, pp. 1440–1518
title: AN ACT to provide for an efficient system of common schools throughout the State.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 260, pp. 1440–1518
summary: This act establishes a comprehensive system for common schools in Kentucky, divided into various articles covering the school fund, board of education, superintendents, districts, taxation, graded common schools, teachers, institutes, libraries, and specifically 'Colored Schools'.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 40, pp. 90–91
title: AN ACT to regulate the travel or transportation of the white and colored passengers on the railroads of this State.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 40, pp. 90–91
summary: This act requires railroad companies operating in Kentucky to provide separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers. Each separate coach or compartment must be clearly marked to indicate the race for which it is designated. The law also mandates that there be no discrimination in the quality, convenience, or accommodations provided for either race.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 65, pp. 133–201
title: AN ACT to regulate elections in this Commonwealth. I. General Provisions.ARTICLE ARTICLE II. Precincts. ARTICLE III. Elections, how conducted. ARTICLE IV. Registration. ARTICLE V. Canvassing returns. ARTICLE VI. Time of holding elections. ARTICLE VII. Vacancies, how filled. ARTICLE VIII. Contested…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1891, ch. 65, pp. 133–201
summary: This statute outlines the process for voter registration in Kentucky cities. It specifies the dates and times for registration, the information to be recorded in the registration book, and the requirements for a person to be registered. Crucially, it mandates that the registration book must record whether an applicant is 'white or colored'.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 100, pp. 253–333
title: AN ACT for the government of cities of the second class in the Commonwealth of Kentucky. ART CLE I. Municipalities.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 100, pp. 253–333
summary: This section mandates the establishment and maintenance of separate schools for white and colored children in cities of the first class. It states that colored schools shall be entitled to the same benefits, governed by the same rules, and subject to the same restrictions as white schools. The statute explicitly mentions 'colored children' and 'white children', indicating a racial segregation in education.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 48, pp. 115–136
title: AN ACT relating to the Asylums for the Insane, and the Institution for Feeble-minded Children, supported by the State.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 48, pp. 115–136
summary: This statute mandates that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same buildings within asylums. It also outlines procedures for admitting and discharging patients, including provisions for pauper idiots and pay patients from other states.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 55, pp. 153–171
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled"An act to provide for an efficient system of common schools throughout the State," approved July sixth, one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 55, pp. 153–171
summary: This statute outlines the process for obtaining teachers' certificates in Kentucky. It mandates separate examination schedules for white and colored teachers, with white teachers examined on the first Friday and Saturday of specified months, and colored teachers on the second Friday and Saturday of the same months. The statute also specifies that the State Board of Examiners shall prepare separate series of questions for white and colored teachers, all of the same grade.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 66, pp. 182–185
title: AN ACT to amend an act to regulate elections in this Commonwealth, approved June thirtieth, one thousand eight hundred and ninety—two.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 66, pp. 182–185
summary: This act amends a previous election regulation act by modifying the form of the registration book. The new form includes a field for 'Color', which was not present in the original form. This addition is significant as it introduces a racial classification into voter registration.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 91, pp. 227–228
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled"An act for the government of cities of the fourth class," approved June twenty-eighth, one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1894, ch. 91, pp. 227–228
summary: This act amends a previous law concerning cities of the fourth class. It mandates that public school funding from the state common school fund be distributed separately to 'white boards of education' and 'colored boards of education' based on the per capita amount for each white child and colored child of pupil age, respectively. It also outlines the process for establishing school districts and appointing trustees in these cities.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, ch. 18, pp. 43–46
title: AN ACT to amend section sixty-three of an act entitled "An act to provide an efficient system of common schools throughout the State," approved July sixth, one thousand eight hundred and ninety -three.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, ch. 18, pp. 43–46
summary: This act amends a previous law regarding teacher certification. It establishes separate examination dates for white and colored teachers, with white teachers examined on the third Friday and Saturday of May, June, July, and August, and colored teachers examined on the fourth Friday and Saturday of the same months. The State Board of Examiners is also required to prepare separate sets of questions for white and colored teachers of the same grade.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, ch. 33, pp. 74–83
title: AN ACT to establish houses of reform, one for boys and one for girls, and to provide for the government thereof and making an appropriation therefor.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, ch. 33, pp. 74–83
summary: This act amends a previous law concerning the protection of food fish. However, a preceding section (§ 20) within the provided text mandates that children of white and colored races committed to the Houses of Reform shall be provided with separate departments. This indicates a segregation policy within correctional institutions.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, ch. 36, pp. 86–88
title: AN ACT concerning the education of children.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, ch. 36, pp. 86–88
summary: This act amends a previous law regarding compulsory education for children. It outlines exemptions for children taught at home, those with physical or mental disabilities, or those excused by trustees. Crucially, it includes a provision that excuses attendance if there is no "white school, in the case of white children, or colored school, in the case of colored children, taught within two miles by the nearest traveled road." This explicitly mandates separate educational facilities based on race and implies unequal access or availability of schools for Black children.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, p. 19
title: Resolution concerning the State Normal School for colored persons
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1896, p. 19
summary: This resolution makes an additional appropriation to extend the grounds and enlarge the buildings of the State Normal School for colored persons.

statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, p. 171
title: District Taxation Under Special Act of Legislature
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, p. 171
summary: This statute addresses district taxation for school purposes in the Robards District. A special act authorized a tax of 75 cents per $100 of property value and $5 per poll to erect buildings and maintain a ten-month school. The act explicitly states it does not apply to negroes or their property, though white taxpayers could not complain on this basis. The statute also details requirements for notice posting, the object of the vote, and the need for a trustee order designating the tax amount, even if not formally recorded.

statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, p. 175
title: E. TOWN SCHOOL DISTRICT vs. L. & N. R. R.
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, p. 175
summary: This case addresses the collection of delinquent taxes owed to school districts. It states that taxes due before November 11, 1892, are to be collected by trustees, while taxes due after that date must be collected by the county superintendent. Crucially, the ruling states that a corporation cannot avoid taxation by claiming it has no color, as all property is taxed except that belonging to colored people. This explicitly indicates a racially discriminatory tax exemption.

summary: This statute outlines the procedures for voter registration in cities, including the appointment and duties of registration officers, the process for challenging a person's right to register, the format of registration books, and the timing of registration. It specifies that registration books should include a column for 'Color'.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1555
title: § 1555. Party affiliation—provisions for registering.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1555, pp. 661–663
summary: This statute outlines the process for holding primary elections in Kentucky. It states that all legal voters have the right to participate, subject to additional political qualifications prescribed by the party committee. It also establishes a system for party affiliation registration, where individuals can declare their party preference on regular state registration books. While not explicitly mentioning race, this statute is classified as Jim Crow because the ability to impose 'additional political qualifications' by party committees, combined with the historical context of racial segregation in the South, allowed for the disenfranchisement of Black voters through discriminatory party rules and practices, effectively limiting their participation in the political process.

statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1, pp. 94–95
title: § 1.The General Assembly shall have no power to pass laws for the emancipation of slaves, without the consent of their owners, or without paying their owners, previous to such emancipation, a full equivalent in money, for the slaves so emancipated, and providing for their removal from the State.…
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1, pp. 94–95; The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1, pp. 93–94
summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines provisions related to slavery and free negroes/mulattoes. It grants the General Assembly power to regulate emancipation, prevent the immigration of free negroes and mulattoes who refuse to leave or return to the state, and punishes such individuals with felony charges and penitentiary confinement. It also addresses the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating that grand jury inquests are not necessary but petit jury trials are still a privilege. The text also includes provisions for the common school fund and the revision of the constitution.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2008
title: § 2008. Appointment of board in counties having cities of first-class—terms of office.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 2008, pp. 824–825
summary: This statute establishes a Board of Children's Guardians in counties with a first-class city. The board is to be composed of six persons, two of whom shall be colored. The board will be a body politic and corporate, responsible for children's guardianship, and its members will be appointed by the judge of the city or police court.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2095a
title: § 2095a. Houses of Reform - appropriation -payment of.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 2095a, pp. 850–856
summary: This statute outlines the operation of Houses of Reform for juveniles under eighteen. It details commitment duration, discharge procedures, educational and vocational instruction, the transfer of minor convicts from the penitentiary, and mandates the separation of white and colored inmates into distinct departments. It also includes provisions for funding and reporting.

title: § 250. Asylum unable to accommodate—patients may be received in another asylum.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 250, p. 280; The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 250, pp. 305–306; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 1, 1915, § 250, pp. 308–309; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 216b-26, p. 137; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 250, p. 313
summary: This statute outlines the procedures for managing the capacity of insane asylums in Kentucky. It details how patient transfers are to be handled to prevent overcrowding and mandates that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same buildings. It also addresses the reception of patients, the role of courts and superintendents, and provisions for discharged patients.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 282
title: § 282. Colored deaf mutes—institution for.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 282, p. 287; The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 282, p. 314
summary: This statute establishes a separate institution for the education of colored deaf mutes at Danville, Kentucky. It mandates that this institution be under the same board of commissioners as the institution for white deaf mutes, but explicitly states that the two races shall be forever kept entirely separate and distinct from each other.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 310
title: § 310. Appropriation—annual for colored children.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 310, p. 293; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 310, p. 162
summary: This statute appropriates funds for the education of colored blind children in Kentucky, establishing a separate appropriation for their sole and exclusive use. It mandates that these funds be expended similarly to those for white blind children and that colored blind children receive equal terms of rights, benefits, and privileges. However, it also states that both races shall be under the same general management and superintendent.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 3219
title: § 3219. School tax.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 3219, pp. 1218–1220
summary: This statute mandates that the board of education shall provide, maintain, and support separate schools for colored children.

title: § 45274. Name of school—president and powers—superintendent.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 45274, p. 1604; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4527a, p. 905; Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1916, § 299, p. 140; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4527a, p. 2481; Baldwin's Kentucky Statute Service, 1922, § 4527a, pp. 802–803
summary: This statute details the renaming of the 'State Normal School for Colored Persons' to 'The Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons'. It outlines the powers and responsibilities of its board of trustees, the selection and duties of the institute's president, and the establishment of a department for agriculture and mechanics. It also specifies admission requirements for pupils, including a pledge to teach in colored common schools.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4527
title: § 4527. Trustees—appointment—term of office—powers—vacancies—treasurer.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4527, pp. 1603–1604; The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4527, pp. 1893–1894; The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, § 419, p. 177; Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 503, pp. 188–189; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4527, pp. 904–905; Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1916, § 290, p. 138; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 4527, pp. 1225–1226; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4527, p. 2481
summary: This statute mandates the segregation of public schools by race, explicitly stating that white children cannot attend schools for colored children, and colored children cannot attend schools for white children. It also establishes a separate normal school for colored persons and outlines its governance. Teachers' institutes are to be organized separately for colored school officers and teachers.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4762
title: § 4762. Judgment—minor to be apprenticed—duty of clerk.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4762, p. 1674
summary: This statute outlines the legal process for identifying, trying, and punishing individuals deemed vagrants. Convicted vagrants over twenty-one years of age could be bound out to labor or sold into servitude for up to twelve months. Minors would be apprenticed until the age of twenty-one. The proceeds from the sale of a vagrant were to be used first for prosecution fees, then to pay the vagrant's debts, and any remainder was to be paid to the wife and children, or the vagrant upon completion of their term. Married men with families could be discharged if they posted bond to support their families and engage in honest work. The statute also details the rights and powers of those who purchased or took in a vagrant.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 796
title: § 796. No discrimination in coaches or compartments.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 796, p. 446; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 796, p. 293; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 796, p. 597; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 796, pp. 597–598; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 796, pp. 699–700
summary: This statute requires railroad companies operating in Kentucky to provide separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers. Each compartment must be divided by a substantial wooden partition with a door and clearly marked with appropriate words indicating the race for which it is designated. The law also stipulates that there should be no discrimination in the quality, convenience, or accommodations provided for either race. Failure to comply results in a misdemeanor charge and a fine for the railroad company. The statute also includes case law interpretations regarding company liability and the constitutionality of the separate coach law.

statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 8, p. 72
title: § 8. In all elections for Representatives, every free male citizen (negroes, mulattoes, and Indians excepted), who at the time being, hath attained to the age of twenty -one years, and resided in the State two years, or the county or town in which he offers to vote one year next preceding the…
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 8, p. 72; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 1, 1915, § 8, p. 56
summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines the qualifications for electors in elections for Representatives. It explicitly excludes 'negroes, mulattoes, and Indians' from the right to vote, while granting suffrage to free male citizens who meet age and residency requirements. It also details the process for representation in the House and Senate.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 120, pp. 311–312
title: AN ACT for the benefit of the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky, and appropriating money to pay existing deficiencies, and to provide additional income therefor.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 120, pp. 311–312
summary: This act appropriates $15,000 annually to the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky. It acknowledges that the college's income from federal land grants and appropriations is reduced by 14% because it must be shared with a "colored normal school" for the maintenance of the Black population. The act also addresses a deficit accumulated by the college due to increased expenditures.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 31, p. 108
title: AN ACT to amend section 1 of an act, entitled "An Act to authorize trustees of county seminary and school property, owned or held in trust by trustees by a majority of their board, to dispose of same to trustees of common school districts embracing same," approved March 17, 1896.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 31, p. 108
summary: This act amends a previous law to allow trustees of county seminaries, established before December 18, 1865, to sell or dispose of seminary property to trustees of white common school districts. The property or its proceeds must be used for the education of white pupils in those districts, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction to compensate for their interest in the seminary property.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 36, pp. 132–134
title: AN ACT to provide for the establishing of graded schools in common school districts bordering on county lines.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 36, pp. 132–134
summary: This act allows for the establishment of graded common school districts by petitioning county judges. It specifies that the election to approve the establishment and taxation for such schools must be held for 'legal white voters' and that taxes can be levied on property belonging to 'said white voters or corporations' or as a poll tax on 'each white male inhabitant over twenty-one years of age'.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 51, pp. 148–150
title: AN ACT creating the thirty-first judicial district of Kentucky, fixing the time of holding courts thereof, providing for the election of a circuit judge and Commonwealth's attorney, and changing the twenty -third and twenty -fourth districts of Kentucky so as to provide for said thirty-first…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 51, pp. 148–150
summary: This act creates a new judicial district (thirty-first) and adjusts existing ones (twenty-third and twenty-fourth) due to population growth and resource development. It also includes a provision for paying patrols, with higher pay in counties over 150,000 inhabitants. The patrol payment is set at a maximum of one dollar per ten hours of duty, or two dollars in larger counties at the court's discretion. Patrols must present claims for services, specifying hours and verified by oath.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 53, pp. 152–154
title: AN ACT to empower cities of the fourth class to separate the management and control of their schools where the same are now under the control of a board of education.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 53, pp. 152–154
summary: This act allows cities of the fourth class in Kentucky to separate their existing graded free schools into distinct white and colored common schools, managed and controlled by a Board of Education. This separation can be enacted by ordinance.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 6, pp. 54–56
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled An act to regulate elections in this Commonwealth, approved June 30, 1892.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 6, pp. 54–56
summary: This act amends a previous election law by expanding the requirement for voter registration to include cities and towns of the fifth and sixth classes. It also mandates that election officers issue a certificate of registration to each voter, and that no person may vote without presenting this certificate.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 85, pp. 204–205
title: AN ACT to prohibit white and colored persons from attending the same school.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 85, pp. 204–205
summary: This act makes it illegal for any person, corporation, or association to operate a college, school, or institution that admits both white and negro races as pupils. Violators face a fine of one thousand dollars, and an additional one hundred dollars for each day the school is operated after conviction. Instructors teaching in such institutions are also subject to the same fines.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 118, pp. 454–457
title: AN ACT to amend section four thousand three hundred and fifteen, Kentucky Statutes.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 118, pp. 454–457
summary: This statute outlines the responsibilities of supervisors in overseeing road work performed by delinquent taxpayers and convicts, including the use of chains to prevent escape. It establishes a system where delinquent taxpayers can work off their fines through labor on roads, which historically has been applied in a racially discriminatory manner.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 156, pp. 542–555
title: AN ACT to amend sections two thousand two hundred and forty-one, two thousand two hundred and forty-two, and two thousand two hundred and forty-three, and repealing and providing a substitute for section two thousand two hundred and forty -seven of the Kentucky Statutes, compiled and edited by John…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 156, pp. 542–555
summary: This statute amends existing laws regarding jury selection in Kentucky, including provisions for separate jury wheels in counties with circuit courts of continuous sessions, which may imply racial segregation in jury selection processes.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 18, pp. 83–100
title: AN ACT creating and establishing a Board of Commissioners, to be known as the Kentucky State Board of Control for Charitable Institutions, and prescribing its duties and powers.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 18, pp. 83–100
summary: This statute outlines the procedures for the reception and care of patients in asylums, explicitly stating that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same building, indicating a racial segregation policy.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 22, pp. 111–271
title: AN ACT relating to Revenue and Taxation.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 22, pp. 111–271
summary: This statute outlines the taxation of railroad and bridge companies in school districts, specifying that the funds collected from white and colored school districts are to be distributed based on the number of white and colored children, thereby reinforcing racial segregation in educational funding.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 51, pp. 316–319
title: AN ACT to repeal chapter two hundred and ninety -six of the Session Acts of eighteen hundred and eighty-seven and eighteen hundred and eignty-eight.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 51, pp. 316–319
summary: This statute establishes the Albany High School as a corporation and outlines its governance, specifically stating that it will receive funding for white children only, thereby enforcing racial segregation in education.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 55, pp. 326–328
title: AN ACT relating to amendment of section one hundred and forty—five of the Constitution, relating to suffrage and elections.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 55, pp. 326–328
summary: This statute amends the Kentucky Constitution to require that individuals must have paid all state, county, municipal, district, and school taxes at least sixty days before an election in order to be eligible to vote. This provision effectively disenfranchises those who cannot afford to pay these taxes, which disproportionately affects Black citizens and other marginalized groups.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 56, pp. 328–329
title: AN ACT appropriating money for industrial training for colored persons and for completing girls' dormitory and providing water for ordinary use and fire protection at Kentucky Normal Industrial Institute.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 56, pp. 328–329
summary: This statute appropriates funds for the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for colored persons, addressing the need for industrial training and improvements to facilities specifically for Black youth.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 57, pp. 329–335
title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled "An act for the government of cities of the first class," approved July first, eighteen hundred and ninety—three.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 57, pp. 329–335
summary: This statute includes provisions for the training of colored youth in industrious habits and useful trades, indicating a segregated approach to education and vocational training.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 59, p. 338
title: AN ACT to make it unlawful to present plays in this Commonwealth that are based upon antagonism alleged formerly to exist between master and slave or that excite race prejudice, and to provide a penalty therefor.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 59, p. 338
summary: This statute makes it unlawful to present plays that are based on the historical antagonism between master and slave or that excite race prejudice, imposing fines and imprisonment for violations.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 56, pp. 150–160
title: AN ACT for the government and regulation of the Common Schools of the State.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 56, pp. 150–160
summary: This act establishes that each county will compose one school district, with an exception for cities or towns that maintain a separate system of public schools. The remaining part of the county outside such a city or town district will constitute a school district. Within thirty days of the act taking effect, county officials will divide each county school district into educational divisions with an equal number of school-aged children, including both white and colored children, based on the last census.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 62, pp. 174–180
title: AN ACT to amend an act approved March the 21st, 1906, entitled, " An Act to establish a system of State Normal Schools in Kentucky; to create a Board of Regents for the general management thereof; to create a Normal Exec nti ve Council, which shall determine the requirements for admission and…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 62, pp. 174–180
summary: This act amends a previous law establishing State Normal Schools in Kentucky. It divides the state into two districts, Eastern and Western, for the Eastern Kentucky State Normal School (Richmond) and the Western Kentucky State Normal School (Bowling Green). The boundaries of these districts are to be determined by a commission based on white population, aiming for districts that are as equal as possible in white population.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 64, pp. 186–187
title: AN ACT for additional improvements at the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 64, pp. 186–187
summary: This act appropriates $40,000 for the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons in Frankfort, Kentucky. The funds are designated for paying outstanding debts from land purchases, and for the erection and equipment of an auditorium, practice school, and mechanical shop.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 71, pp. 225–227
title: AN ACT to amend section 4375 of the Kentucky Statutes, Carroll's Edition, 1903.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 71, pp. 225–227
summary: This act amends a previous law concerning burial associations. The provided text also discusses the apportionment of surplus funds in the State Treasury for white and colored schools, with interest accruing at six percent per annum. It specifies that the per capita derived from this interest shall be apportioned to white and colored schools respectively. The act also addresses the equitable apportionment of surplus funds when new counties are formed from existing ones that have such a surplus.

statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, p. 24
title: Amendment to statute regarding student appointments to the Agricultural and Mechanical College
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, p. 24
summary: This statute amends a previous law to specify that each county in Kentucky is entitled to appoint one white pupil annually to the Agricultural and Mechanical College for every three thousand white school children, and one for each fraction thereof over fifteen hundred, based on the last official census. Each county is guaranteed at least one appointment. The appointed students receive free tuition, matriculation fees, room rent, fuel, and lights, along with other university advantages, except for board.

statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, p. 301
title: General Provisions for Charitable Institutions (Asylums)
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, p. 301
summary: This statute outlines general provisions for charitable institutions, specifically asylums. It mandates that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same building. It also details procedures for admitting and discharging patients, including provisions for pauper idiots, pay patients from other states, and criminal patients. The Board of Control is directed to ensure asylums are kept full and receive their due proportion of patients, while also enforcing racial segregation within the facilities.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1376c
title: § 1376c. 1. Plays that excite race prejudice forbidden—penalty.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1376c, p. 697
summary: This statute makes it unlawful for any person to present, or participate in the presentation of, any play that is based upon antagonism alleged to exist between master and slave, or that excites race prejudice. Violators are subject to a fine or imprisonment, or both.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1399a
title: § 1399a. Slave marriages—children to inherit—children of subsequent marriage.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1399a, p. 703; The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1399a, pp. 703–704; Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 1399a, pp. 339–342
summary: This statute addresses the legitimacy and inheritance rights of children born from slave marriages. It states that children born from cohabitation between enslaved individuals as husband and wife are considered lawful children and legal heirs. However, if either parent later legally marries another person and has children from that subsequent marriage, the children from the slave marriage will only inherit a proportion of the property based on the ratio of children from the slave marriage to children from the subsequent legal marriage. The act also specifies that it does not apply if the property has already been sold to innocent purchasers or divided.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1477a
title: § 1477a. Printed oaths—voter may be required to swear—penalties against voter and election officer.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1477a, pp. 735–736; Kentucky election laws, primary law and Corrupt Practice Act, 1919, § 1477a, pp. 31–33
summary: This statute outlines the process for challenging a voter's qualifications and requires voters to take a detailed oath affirming their age, residency, and lack of felony convictions. It specifies the number of witnesses allowed in a dispute and mandates that the oath be subscribed and sworn before an election judge. The subscribed oath is to be returned to the county clerk and then to the grand jury, with penalties for failure to do so. The oath itself includes specific residency requirements and a declaration of no disqualification.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2971
title: § 2971. Es cheated property—concerning.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 2971, pp. 1296–1299
summary: This statute mandates the separate maintenance and keeping of schools for white and colored children, prohibiting white children from attending schools for colored children and vice versa.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 3588a
title: § 3588a. Graded white and colored schools provision for.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 3588a, pp. 1513–1514; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 3588a, pp. 428–429; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 3588a, p. 2027
summary: This statute allows cities of the fourth class that have already established a system of free graded schools to separate them into distinct white and colored common schools. It mandates that taxes raised from white individuals or corporations cannot be used for colored schools, and vice versa. Each system will be governed by a board of six trustees and supported by a pro rata share of the State School Fund and local taxation.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 3780
title: § 3780.County court to appoint jurisdiction of patrols.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 3780, p. 1598
summary: This statute outlines the appointment, duties, and compensation of patrols in Kentucky counties. County courts are authorized to divide counties into districts and appoint patrols to maintain public peace and order. Patrols are tasked with visiting suspected places and places of unlawful assemblies. Compensation is based on hours of service, with a higher rate for counties with over 150,000 inhabitants. A separate section addresses the appointment of patrolmen in counties with first-class cities, with compensation paid by petitioners or employers.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4372
title: § 4372.School fund can not be ap pro pri-ated or devoted to the payment of teachers not acting under the control or supervision of the officers of the common schools.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4372, pp. 1814–1815
summary: This statute details the distribution and management of the common school fund in Kentucky. It outlines the process for estimating and apportioning funds based on pupil-child census data, the role of the Auditor and Superintendent of Public Instruction, and procedures for handling uncalled-for or unused funds. Crucially, it states that the per capita derived from interest on bonded surplus in the State Treasury shall be duly apportioned to the white and colored schools of the county respectively.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4426a
title: § 4426a. (1) County to compose school district—exceptions.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4426a, pp. 1840–1847; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4426a, p. 843; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4426a, pp. 843–850; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 4426a, pp. 1156–1157; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4426a, pp. 2256–2257; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4426a, pp. 2428–2429
summary: This statute outlines the process for dividing school districts into educational divisions and sub-districts. It explicitly mentions the inclusion of both white and colored children in these divisions and sub-districts. However, it also contains provisions that disproportionately affect Black students, such as the requirement that sub-districts must have at least fifty white children of school age to receive per capita funding for one teacher, and no more than one hundred white pupil-children for the payment of one teacher. This implies a potential underfunding or lack of resources for schools with a higher proportion of Black students.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4427
title: § 4427.(1)Boundary.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4427, p. 1847
summary: This statute outlines the organization and administration of common school districts in Kentucky. It details rules for district boundaries, pupil population requirements, and the establishment of schools. Crucially, it contains a clause stating that 'nothing in this chapter shall be construed to authorize any white person to attend a common school or other institution of learning established for colored children.'

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4439a
title: § 4439a. Seminary property may be acquired by trustees.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4439a, p. 1854; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 4439a, pp. 1171–1172; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4439a, p. 2441
summary: This statute authorizes trustees holding legal title to county seminary property (acquired before December 18, 1865) to sell, transfer, or convey it to the trustees of white common school districts where the seminary property is located. The proceeds or property must be used for the education of white pupils, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction to compensate for their interest in the seminary property.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4441
title: § 4441. Additional tax may be levied to pay indebtedness.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4441, p. 1856
summary: This statute, § 4442, states that a tax levied to pay indebtedness for schoolhouses shall be collected as provided by law for the present school tax. However, it includes a proviso that 'no tax shall be levied or collected from the property of colored persons to pay any indebtedness incurred for the benefit of schools for white children.'

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4464a
title: § 4464a.Graded schools for two counties near line, how established.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4464a, pp. 1868–1869
summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing graded common schools that could span two counties. It specifies that the establishment of such a school and the levying of taxes for its maintenance and construction require a vote of the 'legal white voters' within the proposed district. The statute also details requirements for petitions, approvals from county judges and superintendents, and the proximity of the schoolhouse to the district's boundary.

statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4526a
title: § 4526a. (1) White and colored not to be taught in same college—penalty.
grouped_by: same Ky. St. section; same text
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4526a, p. 1893; Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 4526a, pp. 1186–1190; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4526a, p. 904; Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1916, § 210, pp. 110–111; The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 4526a, p. 1219; Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1922, § 161, pp. 311–312; The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4526a, pp. 2476–2477
summary: This statute mandates the separation of white and colored individuals in educational institutions. It prohibits teaching both races in the same college, school, or institution, with penalties for violations. It also makes it unlawful for individuals of one race to attend schools where the other race is received as pupils, with fines for each day of attendance. Exceptions are made for penal institutions and houses of reform. The law also allows for separate and distinct branches of private institutions in different localities, at least twenty-five miles apart, for the exclusive education of one race.

It outlines admission requirements, including age, health, moral character, and a pledge to teach in colored common schools. Tuition is free for eligible colored residents. The statute also forbids sectarian teaching but promotes Christian morality. It details trustee responsibilities for school inspection and reporting, and specifies annual appropriations for teacher salaries and expenses, as well as a separate appropriation for a dormitory for female pupils. Additional appropriations for buildings and support are noted from earlier acts.

The selection is made by county superintendents. Additionally, it mentions free tuition for students of the ministry at the university's discretion.
